segments.text:
Usage text. The script prints it when the arguments are wrong (line 129).
- `total` is the rate of an interval in this tool: the sum over the threads of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9, in GB/s.
- `I_agg` is the rate that the runner printed for the same interval. It is shown for comparison.
- Part 2 uses only the intervals marked `64+56`.
Modules of the Python standard library. No other package is needed.
Return 0 for a CPU number below 64 and 1 for every other CPU number. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0, and CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
segments.heading: Function `half`: the mesh of a CPU

segments.text: Read the file line by line. A line that starts with `#` is a header or comment line of the runner. The script searches it for `min_ms=`, `stop=` and `thp=`, and it keeps the first value found for each of the three. These values are only shown in the report, and they change no rate.
segments.heading: Function `read_csv`: read one bwx csv file

segments.text:
- Every other line is split at the commas into the list `p`. Python counts from 0, so `p[5]` is field 6.
- A row with `T` in the first field holds one thread in one interval. The key of the interval is (`p[1]`, `p[2]`, `p[3]`): round, position and kernel, kept as text.
- `p[5]` is the CPU that the thread is pinned to. `p[6]` is `bytes`, the number of bytes that the thread read in the interval (a copy kernel counts read plus written bytes). `p[7]` is `elapsed_s` in seconds: the time from the clock read of the thread before its first timed kernel call to its last clock read of the interval [Ref2].
- The rate of the thread is `bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9`, in GB/s.
- `p[-1]` is the last field, `flags`: `-` or `late`. The fields `tid`, `t_sched_s`, `t_start_s`, `t_end_s` and `passes` are not read.
- `threads` keeps the intervals in the order of their first T row, and each interval keeps its threads in file order.

A row with `I` in the first field is the line that the runner prints once per interval. The script keeps only `p[8]`, the field `aggregate_GBps`: the bytes of all threads divided by the longest elapsed time of one thread [Ref1]. All other rows (P rows and C rows) are skipped. The function returns the header values, the thread lists and the I row rates.

The csv files of the folder are read with `read_csv` in the order of their names. For each interval the row holds:
- `folder`, `file`, `round`, `pos`, `kernel`: where the interval comes from. `folder` is the last part of the folder path.
- `threads`: the number of T rows of the interval.
- `total`: the sum of the rates of all these T rows. This is the rate of the interval, in GB/s.
- `I_agg`: the `aggregate_GBps` of the I row with the same key, or no value when the file has no such row.
- `flagged`: the number of T rows whose flag is not `-`. These rows stay in `total`.
- `min_ms`, `stop`, `thp`: the header values of the file.
segments.heading: Function `interval_rows`: one row per interval of a folder

segments.text: The same per mesh. `half` gives the mesh of each thread. For `h` = 0 (CPUs below 64) and `h` = 1 (CPUs from 64 up) the row gets the number of threads, the sum of their rates, and the lowest and the highest rate of one thread.

`is_64_56` is true when four tests hold: 64 threads on CPUs below 64, 56 threads on CPUs from 64 up, no CPU number above 119, and 120 different CPU numbers. This is the whole-chip layout of the test: one thread on each of the CPUs 0-119. `summarize` uses only the intervals that pass.

Keep only the rows with `is_64_56` true. Group them by the kernel name alone, in the order in which each kernel first appears. Round, position and file are not part of the group. So all intervals of one kernel in `rows` form one group, whichever kernel ran before them.
segments.heading: Function `summarize`: statistics per kernel

segments.text:
One result row per kernel, computed over the `total` values `v` of its group:
- `n`: the number of intervals. `min` and `max`: the lowest and the highest total.
- `median`: the middle value. For an even `n` it is the mean of the two middle values. It is not rounded here.
- `values`: the totals in file order.
- `flagged`: the sum of the flagged T rows of these intervals.
- `files`, `min_ms`, `stop`, `thp`: the different file names and header values of these intervals, each list sorted.

Return a value with every floating-point number in it rounded to 3 decimals (0.001 GB/s for a rate). Lists and dictionaries are handled element by element. Only the JSON output uses this function (line 142).
segments.heading: Function `rounded`: 3 decimals for the JSON output

segments.text: Text of one mesh in a Part 1 line: the sum of the rates, the thread count, and the lowest and the highest rate of one thread. A mesh without a thread prints `-`.
segments.heading: Function `fmt_half`: text of one mesh column

segments.text: Print a line of column names, then one line per kernel: `n`, then `min`, `median` and `max` with 2 decimals (GB/s), the `min_ms` values, the number of flagged T rows, and every total in file order.
segments.heading: Function `print_summary`: the Part 2 table

segments.text: Arguments that start with `--` are flags. All other arguments are folders. Without a folder, or with a flag other than `--json` and `--pool`, the script prints the usage text and ends with exit status 1.
segments.heading: Function `main`: arguments, statistics, output

segments.text: For each folder, build the interval rows with `interval_rows`. The script stops when the csv files of a folder hold no T row. `summarize` then builds the statistics of that folder. With `--pool`, `summarize` runs once more over the rows of all folders together, under the folder name `POOLED`.

With `--json`, print one JSON object and return. `intervals` holds every interval row of every folder, also the rows that are not 64+56. `summary` holds the statistics per folder, then the pooled ones. `rounded` rounds every number to 3 decimals first.

Text output, per folder, under a title line with the folder name:
- Part 1: a line with the file name and its header values, a line of column names, then one line per interval. The line shows round, position, kernel, thread count, `total` with 2 decimals, the two mesh columns from `fmt_half`, `I_agg`, `yes` or `no` for 64+56, and the flagged count.
- Part 2: the table of `print_summary` for this folder.
With `--pool`, print the pooled table with `print_summary` after the last folder.
Run `main` with the command-line arguments when the file is started as a script. When another script imports the file, `main` does not run.
